summary: Presents a performance evaluation of the Maximum Allocation and Russian Dolls bandwidth constraints models described in RFC 3564 for Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering. It examines how the two models behave under different operating conditions, such as blocking and preemption of label switched paths. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Two teachers have different rules for sharing classroom supplies. This memo tests both rules in many situations to see which works better, and reports what happened.

questions: how do mpls bandwidth constraints work
when to use russian dolls or maximum allocation model
subtitle: Testing two bandwidth allocation schemes for prioritized network traffic

tldr.problem: Networks need to allocate bandwidth fairly among different traffic classes (voice, video, best-effort data) without wasting capacity or letting high-priority traffic starve when the network is overloaded.
tldr.mechanism: Two models limit how much bandwidth each traffic class can claim: the Russian Dolls Model stacks classes in priority order, while the Maximum Allocation Model gives each class a fixed limit. This RFC tests both under normal and overload conditions.
tldr.outcome: Russian Dolls shares bandwidth more efficiently but couples classes together; Maximum Allocation isolates classes better but wastes capacity. Neither is universally best; operators must choose based on their traffic and priorities.

facts.label: Models evaluated
facts.value: Maximum Allocation Model (MAM) and Russian Dolls Model (RDM)

facts.label: Operating scenarios
facts.value: Normal load, overload, partial preemption, pure blocking, complete sharing

today: RFC 4128 is an Informational RFC documenting performance evaluation results. MPLS and Diffserv remain widely used in carrier networks. The bandwidth constraints models described here guide how operators dimension their networks for quality of service, though modern networks may use additional techniques like segment routing or traffic engineering based on application requirements.

sections.title: Why networks need bandwidth classes
sections.content:
Modern networks carry different types of traffic with different importance. A voice call is urgent and intolerant of delay; a video stream needs steady high bandwidth; bulk data transfers can wait. Differentiated Services (Diffserv) marks packets with a class of service, and MPLS Traffic Engineering (TE) uses that marking to reserve and forward Label Switched Paths (LSPs—pre-planned routes) for each class separately.

The challenge is deciding how much bandwidth each class can claim. Allocate too much to voice and video, and data transfers starve. Allocate too little to high-priority traffic and expensive voice calls get dropped. This RFC presents a performance evaluation of two competing Bandwidth Constraints Models (BCMs) to help operators choose the right approach for their network.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of an internet service provider managing a pipe with three customers: Alice wants fast video delivery, Bob wants reliable voice calls, and Carol just wants to send email when the others aren't busy. How much pipe should each get so everyone is happy?

sections.title: Two competing bandwidth models
sections.content:
The Maximum Allocation Model (MAM) assigns a hard limit to each traffic class independently. For example, voice gets up to 6 units of bandwidth, video gets up to 7, and data gets up to 15 on a link with total capacity 15. The constraint for each class is separate: N1 ≤ B1 (voice cannot exceed 6) and N2 ≤ B2 (video cannot exceed 7), with an aggregate limit that N1 + N2 + N3 ≤ 15. Higher-priority classes can preempt lower ones if the network is full.

The Russian Dolls Model (RDM) thinks in nested groups. It says: voice can use up to 6 units; voice plus video together can use up to 11 units; all three classes together can use the full 15 units. Lower-priority traffic sits inside the larger allocation for higher-priority traffic. The constraints are: N1 ≤ B1 (≤ 6), N1 + N2 ≤ B2 (≤ 11), and N1 + N2 + N3 ≤ B3 (= 15). This allows classes to "borrow" unused bandwidth from classes they sit inside, increasing sharing.

The RFC evaluates both models by simulating networks under varying load: normal operation, overload (too much traffic), partial preemption (some classes can be bumped off), complete blocking (no preemption), and complete sharing (no restrictions). The goal is to understand when each model meets service objectives for blocking probability and preemption rate.
sections.plainLanguage: MAM is like giving each student their own pencil box with a number painted on it: Alice's box holds max 6 pencils, Bob's holds 7, Carol's holds 15. RDM is like stacking boxes: Alice's 6-pencil box sits in Bob's 11-pencil box, which sits in Carol's 15-pencil box. Both methods protect Alice and Bob, but RDM lets them share better if one is not using their pencils.

sections.title: How the models behave under normal load and overload
sections.content:
When the network operates at engineered load (traffic volume for which it was designed), both models can deliver comparable blocking probability (the rate at which new calls are rejected) and preemption probability (the rate at which existing calls are interrupted). The RFC shows this using a concrete example: a link with 15-unit capacity, voice load of 2.7 erlangs, video load of 3.5 erlangs, and data load of 3.5 erlangs. Under these conditions, both MAM and RDM achieve similar service-level objectives.

When load increases above engineered levels, the models differ significantly. MAM provides isolation: voice and video can use their separate pools, so an overload of data traffic does not affect voice. RDM provides coupling: because classes share limits, an overload of voice can steal bandwidth from video, even though video is also busy. Under overload, voice performance stays steady in MAM but degrades in RDM. Conversely, RDM protects data better because of the cascaded nesting.

When preemption is disabled (pure blocking), the priorities reverse. RDM's cascaded arrangement now favors higher-priority classes unfairly—voice gets better performance than it deserves. MAM continues to treat classes roughly equally. The RFC shows that the right bandwidth model depends on operational needs: networks expecting overload should prefer MAM for class isolation, while networks with predictable load can use RDM to maximize efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: Under normal conditions, both models work fine—everyone gets what they need and nobody complains. When something goes wrong (too much voice traffic), MAM keeps video unaffected because it has its own pool, but RDM causes video to suffer because it shares space with voice. Which is better depends on what you fear most: wasting space in good times (MAM) or having one class hurt another in bad times (RDM).

sections.title: Trade-off between efficiency and protection
sections.content:
The RFC highlights a fundamental trade-off: bandwidth sharing achieves higher link efficiency (fewer wasted capacity), while class isolation protects classes from interfering with each other. RDM allows greater sharing through its nested structure, leading to better overall link utilization under normal load. MAM imposes isolation, leading to lower efficiency but more predictable per-class performance. When all restrictions are removed (Complete Sharing Model), a link can support more traffic, but lower-priority classes starve under overload.

The choice depends on the operator's priorities. Under normal load, RDM performs better because it wastes less bandwidth. If the network is engineered with adequate capacity for each class, coupling is minimal. However, when networks encounter unexpected surges (a major event triggering many calls), RDM couples the problem across classes, while MAM contains it. The RFC concludes that optimizing solely for link efficiency (the Complete Sharing Model) is dangerous: it maximizes blocking for lower-priority classes under stress, which may violate service-level agreements.

Preemption introduces another dimension. When enabled, both models allow high-priority traffic to displace lower-priority traffic. MAM is insensitive to preemption mode: whether class 1 can preempt class 2, or only class 3, the result is similar because classes have fixed pools. RDM is sensitive: the preemption topology matters because of sharing. Operators must carefully configure preemption rules and test their model under expected conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: RDM is like a food bank where people can share extra food they do not use—efficient but chaotic if supply runs short. MAM is like fixed food rations per family—wasteful if someone gets more than they eat, but fair if food is scarce. For a stable neighborhood, RDM wins. For a crisis, MAM wins.

sections.title: Configuration and robustness
sections.content:
The RFC stresses that bandwidth constraints must be configured correctly by authorized personnel. If an operator mistakenly sets class 2 BC to allow preemption of class 1, the priority inversion will silently cause high-priority calls to drop when they should not. Similarly, if preemption levels are misconfigured on a single router, LSP setup requests may be unnecessarily blocked or existing calls unnecessarily preempted, degrading service unpredictably.

The choice of BCM also depends on whether the network uses preemption. MAM works well with or without preemption enabled. RDM requires careful preemption tuning to avoid unexpected interactions. The RFC notes that each BCM must be dimensioned independently: using MAM parameters to design RDM (or vice versa) will result in incorrect performance, as the models operate by fundamentally different rules.
sections.plainLanguage: If you set the rules wrong, your phone system will break in ways nobody expects. And mixing the rules from one system into another is like trying to play chess with poker chips—it looks similar but does not work.
